## C.4. The ensemble complexity

It is important to note that combining directly interpretable models (weak learners) induces the loss of the interpretability. For example, tree-based ensemble models by bagging (random forest) or boosting (adaboost, gradient boosting, XGboost) are not directly interpretable even if based on simple decision trees, as each tree only sees a subpart of the data and that their outputs are combined.

Stacking models also makes the system non-directly interpretable, even if, once again, every stacked models are simple models.

## C.5. Performance/Interpretability Trade-off

Often, more complex models give better performance. Especially for complex datasets, XGBoost for example will perform better than a simple decision tree. But that added complexity leads to the loss of the interpretability. We talk about the Performance / Interpretability Trade-off.

Source: figure from Arrieta et al. 2019 that you can find here: Re (PDF) Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI): Concepts, Taxonomies, Opportunities and Challenges toward Responsible AI

We highly recommend reading this paper for more information on the subject.

There is no general guideline to follow to resolve this trade-off, it is a case-by-case consideration to make. Depending on the risk/criticality for the users of the model you are building and the regulation in place, you might not have a choice to go for a directly interpretable algorithm. In the other cases, it is always better to start simple and to increase the complexity until reaching a satisfying level of performance.

<!-- PageBreak -->

# D. Toolboxes for indirect interpretability

There are many tools to 'open the black box' and get information about the model, but keep in mind that there are all indirect variable estimations and are just indications and certainly not exact information.

Most of these techniques are universal (model agnostic) and can be applied to all algorithms/models. However, certain tools are better suited for certain types of data and certain type of models. We will mainly focus on two toolboxes: Lime and SHAP as there are the ones most widely used.

## D.1. Structured data

For structured data, and for models that are not directly interpretable, we suggest the use of these two toolboxes, LIME and Shap.

## D.1.a. LIME

The acronym LIME stands for Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations. It provides local interpretability for your classifications and can be applied to any model. It is based on this paper : https://arxiv.org/pdf/1602.04938.pdf and you can also watch this video for a high-level explanation : KDD2016 paper 573

LIME uses a local surrogate model trained on perturbations of the data point we are investigating for explanations.

Source : https://github.com/marcotcr/lime

Even though we can use any interpretable model as the local surrogate, the paper uses a Lasso regression to induce sparsity in explanations.

The advantages of the technique are:

· Both the methodology and the explanations are very intuitive to explain to a human being.

· It is Model-agnostic.

. It works for structured as well as unstructured data (more on that later).

· Available in R and Python (original implementation by the authors of the paper).

<!-- PageBreak -->

Here is how the algorithm works:

· In order to find an explanation for a single data point and a given classifier, it samples the locality around the selected single data point uniformly and at random and generate a dataset of perturbed data points with its corresponding prediction from the model we want to explain.

· Then it uses the specified feature selection methodology to select the number of features that is required for the explanation.

· It calculates the sample weights using a kernel function and a distance function (this captures how close or how far are the sampled points from the original point).

· It then fits an interpretable model (the Lasso regression) on the perturbed dataset using the sample weights to weigh the objective function.

· Finally, it provides local explanations using the newly trained interpretable model.

It provides nice visualizations of the local interpretability like this example taken from this tutorial : Tutorial - continuous and categorical features from LIME's authors:

This is analyzing the Iris dataset, with a Random Forest, after training an 'explainer' like that:

explainer = lime. lime_tabular. LimeTabularExplainer (train, feature_names=iris. feature_names,

class_names=iris. target_names, discretize_continuous=True)

exp = explainer. explain_instance (test [i], rf.predict_proba, num_features=2, top_labels=1)

This figure tells you that, for this instance,(1) the Random Forest model predicted the label 'setosa' with a probability of 1 (left part of the image), (2) it did no because the petal width was smaller or equal to 0.30cm and its length less than 1.6cm (central part of the image) and (3) it gives you the feature values highlighting the important features.

For more details, you can look at:

. The tutorial: Tutorial - continuous and categorical features

## D.1.c. Other methods

They are many other interpretability methods, we will not get into the details, we will refer you to this online book by Christoph Molnar: Interpretable Machine Learning

We will still list them here to be exhaustive.

### Global Model-Agnostic Methods:

· The partial dependence plot is a feature effect method.

· Accumulated local effect plots is another feature effect method that works when features are dependent.

<!-- PageBreak -->

· Feature interaction (H-statistic) quantifies to what extent the prediction is the result of joint effects of the features.

· Functional decomposition is a central idea of interpretability and a technique that decomposes the complex prediction function into smaller parts.

· Permutation feature importance measures the importance of a feature as an increase in loss when the feature is permuted.

· Global surrogate models replaces the original model with a directly interpretable model for interpretation.

· Prototypes and criticisms are representative data point of a distribution and can be used to enhance interpretability.

Local Model-Agnostic Methods:

· Individual conditional expectation curves are the building blocks for partial dependence plots and describe how changing a feature changes the prediction.

· Scoped rules (anchors) are rules that describe which feature values anchor a prediction, in the sense that they lock the prediction in place.

· Counterfactual explanations explain a prediction by examining which features would need to be changed to achieve a desired prediction.

· Shapley values are an attribution method that fairly assigns the prediction to individual features.

### And of course:

· Local surrogate models (LIME) explain a prediction by replacing the complex model with a locally interpretable surrogate model.

· SHAP is another computation method for Shapley values, but also proposes global interpretation methods based on combinations of Shapley values across the data.

If you don't want to read a whole book, here are two papers reviewing the subject:

· PNAS

· NCBI - WWW Error Blocked Diagnostic

#### D.2. Text

We have seen the different toolboxes and methods for tabular, structured data, but how can you do for text? It can be very important to know what words have been critical in order to: assign a sentiment to the sentence, categorize a text or whatever your NLP task was.

LIME and SHAP propose solutions specific to NLP. We will look into them and add another option too.

## D.2.a. LIME

<!-- PageBreak -->

lime

The same way that LIME has a tabular explainer, it also has a text explainer ( package - lime 0.1 documentation ).

You initiate the explainer, after having trained a model for sentient analysis for example:

class_names=['negative', 'positive'] explainer = LimeTextExplainer(class_names=class_names)

And you get the explainer to explain an instance ('text'):

exp = explainer. explain_instance(text, model. predict_proba, num_features=6) And you get that illustration:

It gives you the usual LIME plot with the prediction probabilities of the model for this prediction (on the left) and what were the features (here words) important for the prediction.

This important addition is the highlighted text at the bottom of the figure, that shows you the words, in the sentence, that were important, color coded as a function of the possible labels (here blue for positive, orange for negative sentiment).

As for tabular data, LIME is easy to use and relatively fast.

## D.2.b. SHAP

The process with SHAP is very similar, there are just more visualization options. You

can access the documentation here : Text examples - SHAP latest documentation , from which we took the following examples.

You start with the explainer on your pretrained model: explainer = shap. Explainer (pred)

You compute the shap values for a specific instance: shap_values = explainer (data [ ' text ' ] [ : 0] )

And you visualize the result: shap. plots. text (shap_values)

<!-- PageBreak -->

You have here the different possible labels at the top, with the predicted label highlighted, then the classical SHAP force plot in the middle, and the sentence with important words highlighted at the bottom.

Additionally, you can look at the important words for a single class ('joy' in this example) by averaging the shap values.

shap.plots.bar(shap_values[ :,:,"joy"].mean(0))

For further understanding of the use of SHAP for NLP, you can read this paper: https://openreview.net/pdf?id=yqu82n5FZ9r

### D.2.c. Attention Interpretability

Quite often nowadays, deep neural networks are used for NLP tasks. This allows for specific interpretability if you use attention networks. Indeed, attention layer in a neural network can give you insight into the model's prediction by obtaining the weights in a specific layer. It works for example with BERT and other Transformers.

The interpretability power of these methods is under discussion, we won't go into the details here, but you should know it is a possibility.

Here are some more or less scientific papers about this:

· https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.11218.pdf

. https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2021/papers/Chefer_Transformer_ Interpretability_Beyond_Attention_Visualization_CVPR_2021_paper.pdf

· Deconstructing BERT, Part 2: Visualizing the Inner Workings of Attention

· https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.04840.pdf

## D.3. Images

As for text, images also have specific functions from LIME and SHAP, and also, attention layers of some Deep Learning Networks can be used.

## D.3.a. LIME

As for tabular data, LIME generates perturbations in order to see the impact on the model decision and see what part of the image is crucial for the prediction. Here is an illustration of the process:

<!-- PageBreak -->

The way to implement LIME for image is similar to everything we have seen before. Here we use an example for their official tutorial (Lime Images ), which is based on inception v3. We will look at the interpretability of this image:

The multilabel predictions for the top 5 classes are: 286 Egyptian cat 0.000892741

242 EntleBucher 0.0163564

239 Greater Swiss Mountain dog 0.0171362 241 Appenzeller 0.0393639 240 Bernese mountain dog 0.829222

Let's look at how to visualize the interpretation. First initiate the Explainer and get the explanation:

explainer = lime_image. LimeImageExplainer () explanation = explainer . explain_instance (image, predict_fn, top_labels=5, hide_color=0, num_samples=1000)

Now let see the explanation for the top class (Bernese mountain dog)

from skimage. segmentation import mark_boundaries

temp, mask = explanation. get_image_and_mask(240, positive_only=True, num_features=5, hide_rest=True) plt.imshow(mark_boundaries(temp / 2 + 0.5, mask))

We can also look at the part of the image in favor (green) and in disfavor (red) of the top class:

temp, mask = explanation.get_image_and_mask (240, positive_only=False, num_features=10, hide_rest=False) plt.imshow (mark_boundaries (temp / 2 + 0.5, mask) )

You will find more information on this and the rest of LIME in their paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1602.04938.pdf

SHAP

There are two ways to get interpretability of images with SHAP.

<!-- PageBreak -->

The first one, is with a DeepExplainer. Here is an example using the MNIST databased and a CNN model.

import shap import numpy as np # select a set of background examples to take an expectation over background = x_train [np. random. choice (x_train. shape [0], 100, replace=False) ]

# explain the model's predictions using SHAP (same syntax works for LightGBM, CatBoost, scikit-learn, transformers, Spark, etc.) explainer = shap. Explainer (model)

<!-- PageBreak -->

shap_values = explainer (X)

The first interesting plot is the Waterfall: # visualize the first prediction's explanation shap.plots.waterfall (shap_values [0] )

You can see the influence of each feature, with their direction and magnitude.

Another, more condensed way to illustrate the same thing is the 'force plot': # visualize the first prediction's explanation with a force plot shap.plots. force (shap_values [0])

This is probably the most used visualization of the library.

To understand how a single feature effects the output of the model, we can plot the SHAP value of that feature vs. the value of the feature for all the examples in a dataset. It is a similar approach to Partial Dependency Plot (PDP). In the example here, we are looking at the effect of the number of rooms ('RM') # create a dependence scatter plot to show the effect of a single feature across

the whole dataset shap. plots . scatter (shap_values [ :, "RM"], color=shap_values)

Since SHAP values represent a feature's responsibility for a change in the model output, this plot represents the change in predicted house price as RM (the average number of rooms per house in an area) changes. You can try to understand the variability observed for a single value of RM with its interaction effects with other features. To help reveal these interactions we can color by another feature. If we pass the whole explanation tensor to the color argument the scatter plot will pick the best feature to color by. In this case it picks RAD (index of accessibility to radial highways) since that highlights that the average number of rooms per house has less impact on home price for areas with a high RAD value.

SHAP can also give you the global interpretability of your model.

<!-- PageBreak -->

To do so, we can plot the SHAP values of every feature for every sample. This can be done with the Beeswarm plot. It sorts features by the sum of SHAP value magnitudes over all samples, and uses SHAP values to show the distribution of the impacts each feature has on the model output. The color represents the feature value (red high, blue low). This reveals for example that a high LSTAT (% lower status of the population) lowers the predicted home price. # summarize the effects of all the features shap.plots.beeswarm (shap_values)

Finally, we can also just take the mean absolute value of the SHAP values for each feature to get a standard 'feature importance' bar plot: shap.plots. bar (shap_values)

It is important to note that SHAP designed specific solution for Tree based models (all the way to XGBoost), with their shap.TreeExplainer(model).

We won't go into the details here, but you can find the documentation here : Tabular examples - SHAP latest documentation, and their Nature paper on the subject here: https://www.nature.com/articles/s42256-019-0138-9

Overall, SHAP is a very good library, offering many ways to visualize your interpretability compared to LIME, so why consider LIME? As we already mentioned, the advantage of LIME over SHAP is SPEED. The two methods emerge very differently. LIME perturbs data around an individual prediction to build a model, while SHAP has to compute all permutations globally to get local accuracy.

# B. Of what?

We can be interested to have interpretability of the whole system or just of different parts of the system. We can look to understand a single prediction, all predictions, a part of the model, the whole model, the path that the data takes along the processing pipeline ...

## B.1. Global and Local

<!-- PageBreak -->

There are two main information that we want to access when we talk about Interpretability. We want to access what factors influenced each prediction and with what extend, that is called the Local Interpretability, and we also want to know what the factors of importance for the model are, that is the Global Interpretability.

In the case of simple algorithms like the regressions, the global interpretability is directly given by the coefficients of the model after training (remember to scale or normalize your data first, overwise you will not be able to interpret the results). With sklearn, just use 'model.coef_'. You can put them in a DataFrame with the variable names for simpler visualization :

pd. DataFrame ( {"Feature" : X_train . columns . tolist () , "Coefficients" : model . coef [0]})

In the case of more complex models, we will need to use additional tools to have access to an approximation of this information, like Lime or Shap or the Feature Importance function of sklearn. N.B. LIME and SHAP are local interpretability methods but they can still be used for the global interpretability.

You can refer to the sklearn MOOC part on feature importance here for more

information: Feature importance - Scikit-learn course

For the interpretability of the predictions (local), we see the same distinction between simple and more complex algorithms. With the simple models, we can directly apply the coefficients or the rules (for simple decision tree) to the data specific for each individual prediction. For more complex algorithms, we will again use additional tools (Lime, Shap ... ).

We will come back to the tools in more details in a dedicated section.

# C. Why not interpretable?

## C.1. The data complexity

There are different ways in which the data itself can make the system hard to interpret.

Some variables may contain information that is difficult to comprehend, for example medical or scientific information or expert technical measurements.

Moreover, during the Feature Engineering of the model construction, we may apply manipulations to the data that may lead to a loss of meaning. For example taking the log of a measure, using a dimension reduction method (i.e. PCA), combining variables ...

<!-- PageBreak -->

Finally, the storage of the data can add to the complexity if we lose the lineage and the contextual information that goes with it.

## C.2. The mathematical complexity

As quickly mentioned earlier, a few algorithms are directly interpretable by their mathematical nature. There are 3 of them: the linear regression, the logistic regression and the simple decision tree. By getting the regression coefficients we have direct access to the feature importance foe the model (global interpretability) and we can apply those coefficients to each prediction to get the local interpretability. The decision tree also gives us directly the underlying rules of the model.

On the other hand, many algorithms are not directly interpretable, that is the case of most models used : Ensemble models (Random Forest, XGBoost ... ), SVM, Artificial Neural Networks ... In these cases, we have to use additional toolboxes like Lime or Shap (that we will describe later) to access the model and prediction interpretability.

It is important to note that already existing regulations (for finance and insurance for example) and the one to come from the UE impose the use of directly interpretable models for critical systems i.e. the ones with a potential effect on users' interests.

## C.3. Direct interpretability

## CUSTOMER STORIES: FOSTERING TRANSPARENCY IN DATA SCIENCE FOR ACCELERATED INNOVATION IN BEAUTY TECHNOLOGY

. Challenge: Our client, leader of the beauty industry, needed to rationalize and formalize their Data Science capabilities by implementing standards and best practices, as well as a registry of the different AI models.

. Approach: We helped them build a platform, write the standards (including Responsible Al) and write Model Cards for each model deployed within the company. We also created and moderated a Data Scientist community around this platform to share experience and grow together.

. Outcome: These changes allowed them to step up the development of new projects, improve their quality and ensure greater control of Al initiatives.

<!-- PageFooter: page 11 -->

<!-- PageHeader: Ekimetrics. -->

## TYPES OF INTERPRETABILITY AI FAILURE:

- BLACK BOX EFFECT

- UNSTABLE SYSTEM

- LEGAL RISK

## WHO'S IN CHARGE?

CDO DATA TEAMS

## 3· Interpretability pillar

### Core concept

Ensure access to the factors (characteristics and/or variables) that determine a model's decisions and/or predictions

### What are the risks?

· For your business customers > inability to explain model decisions/predictions. Example: what factors enable an algorithm to establish a medical diagnosis? Or refuse a loan?

· For your end customers > discrimination, prejudice against the legal right to know the factors leading to the decision/prediction (black box effect).

· For your organization > loss of control over your model (black box effect), legal and compliance risks, business risks

Where do you start? For directly interpretable algorithms:

V Use simple regressions and decision trees

For algorithms that are not directly interpretable:

V Add control libraries or algorithmic layers to determine how the model works (Lime and Shape are frequently used tools)

What's the competitive advantage?

· For your customers > trust

· For your organization > control your system, compliance, rigorous customer service (= giving objective reasons to end customers)

## WHAT IS A "BLACK BOX EFFECT"?

It's the inability to explain how an algorithmic model makes its decisions. In other words, it's providing the link between the initial data and the final decision.

## DIRECTLY, NOT DIRECTLY INTERPRETABLE: WHAT'S THE DIFFERENCE?

# 3- Interpretability

Machine Learning changed the way computer programs are done. Developers used to formalize a problem and code the rules that would transform input data into output data. Now, it is the model that determines the rules that link the input and output data through iterations and error minimization. It is this ability that gives all its power to Machine Learning and allows us to solve problems that exceed human formalization capabilities. But it is also coupled with a constraint: the rules applied by the model after training to make its predictions and decision may evade human control. For certain types of models, these rules sometimes remain unknown, even if interpretability techniques have made great progress in recent years. This is the famous "black box effect". However, when we decide to use Al to make decisions or make predictions that will have an impact on the lives of citizens, it is crucial, and soon to be regulatory, to keep control of the models and guarantee their explicability.

The interpretability of AI models is therefore becoming a major challenge, both for those who design them and for those who use them. It is a question of knowing which factors influence each decision and prediction (local interpretability) but also which rules govern the model in general (global interpretability).

Interpretability can be defined as having access to the features or variables that are driving the decisions or predictions of a model.

An Interpretable system becomes:

· Explicable: we can provide information and explanation (see the Explicability section)

· Transparent: it has a functioning intelligible to a human

· Provable: it can provide proof of the accuracy of the result

Whatever your use-case, it is critical to use interpretability methods.

If your system is critical, you should use directly interpretable models (regressions or simple decision trees), you can refer to Section 3.C.Direct Interpretability for more information.

If you are not required Direct Interpretability, are decided to use more complex models, you can use toolboxes to access indirect interpretability. You can refer to Section 3.D for more information, depending on the type of data (tabular, text or images).

## A. For whom?

<!-- PageBreak -->

### A.1. The regulator

As mentioned in the section about legal risks in Introduction, the new European law on AI will describe different levels of criticality for AI models. Depending on the level, complete or partial interpretability will be asked by law and in addition to documentation, some audits might occur. Therefore, interpretability will become mandatory for many AI models.

### A.2. The developer or Data Scientist

The data scientist needs to access, as best as possible, the parameters of a model to understand it, to fix possible mistakes, to improve its performance and to stay in control.

#### A.3. The main user

The user needs information in order to best use the product or solution as well as to trust its recommendation. Adoption is driven by trust and very linked to the information that will be provided. We will get into more details about that in the Explicability section of these Guidelines.

#### A.4. The final user

The final user is the person who is the subject of the prediction or decision. That can be the same person as the main user or a different one. For example, we can have a skin diagnostic solution for doctors (main users) that concerns their patients (final users). This group of people may ask for information about the decision/prediction of the algorithm and in many case, they have the legal right to know what were the factor that lead to the decision/prediction.

<!-- PageFooter: D.1.b. SHAP -->
<!-- PageBreak -->

SHAP stands for SHapley Additive explanations. They define their approach as: 'is a game theoretic approach to explain the output of any machine learning model. It connects optimal credit allocation with local explanations using the classic Shapley values from game theory and their related extensions'. We are going to try to be a bit clearer but it is definitely less intuitive than LIME.

Game theory is a theoretical framework for social situations among competing players. It is the science of optimal decision-making of independent and competing actors in a strategic setting. A "Game" is any situation in which there are several decision-makers, and each of them wants to optimize their results. The optimizing decision will depend on the decisions of others. The game identifies the players' identities, preferences, and available strategies and how these strategies affect the outcome.

In essence, Game Theory is a way to mathematically model complex human behavior, to try to understand it, and predict it. You can read more about game theory and it's fit in the AI world in this article : Game (Theory) for AI? An Illustrated Guide for Everyone .

Applied to Machine Learning, we know that each value of an independent variable or a feature for a given sample is a part of a cooperative game where we assume that prediction is actually the payout. So, let's use an example to understand this in detail.

Assume the following scenario:

We have trained a machine learning model to predict apartment prices in Paris. For a certain apartment, our model predicts 250K euros and we need to explain this prediction. This apartment is 75m2, 2 bedrooms, on the 3rd floor. The average prediction for all apartments is 210K euros. How much has each feature value contributed to the prediction compared to the average prediction?

Now, if we talk in terms of Game Theory, the "game" here is the prediction task for a single instance of the dataset. The "players" are the feature values of the instance that collaborate to play the game (predict a value).

In our example, the feature values 'square_meters, nb_bedrooms and floor' worked together to achieve the prediction of 250K euros. Our goal is to explain the difference between the actual prediction (250K euros) and the average prediction (210K euros): a difference of 40K euros.

A possible explanation could be 'square_meters' contributed 20K euros, 'nb_bedrooms' contributed 10K euros, and 'floor' contributed 10K euros. The contributions add up to 40K - the prediction minus the average predicted house price.

<!-- PageBreak -->

The Shapley value for each variable (payout) is basically trying to find the correct weight such that the sum of all Shapley values is the difference between the predictions and average value of the model. In other words, Shapley values correspond to the contribution of each feature towards pushing the prediction away from the expected value.

Here is the intuitive explanation of the Shapley values, for more details please refer to :

· The Shap librairy documentation:

Welcome to the SHAP documentation - SHAP latest documentation

· The github page:

GitHub - shap/shap: A game theoretic approach to explain the output of any machine learning model.

· A good article explaining how it works:

Interpretable Machine Learning using SHAP-theory and applications

· And this article for a slightly different view:

Understanding SHAP for Interpretable Machine Learning

Computing shapley values takes more time than LIME, but the library comes with more useful types of visualizations that we will describe here. The examples used are coming from their github (GitHub - shap/shap: A game theoretic approach to explain the output of any machine learning model. )

There are different methods of shapley values approximation depending on the type of method we are trying to explain : KernelSHAP, DeepSHAP and TreeSHAP.

First of all, using SHAP is extremely easy, and it can be used on any model. Here is a snipet of code for XGBoost on the Boston Housing Dataset: import xgboost

import shap # train an XGBoost model

X, y = shap.datasets.boston ()

model = xgboost. XGBRegressor () . fit (X, y)

# 4- Explicability

As described in introduction, AI is a system, with users to take into account and an interface to build. Once you have access to what factor influenced your prediction/decision, it comes the time to explain it to your users. That is what explicability is. Knowing your users, understanding not only their needs but their reluctances, choosing the right level of information, giving them control and ability to give feedbacks, all of these techniques will ensure more trust and adoption of your solution.

# A. UX studies

You need to know the appetite of users relative to AI to deliver the right level of explicability.

With explicability, we enter into UX Design and question the preference of users in terms of presentation of results. The level of explicability that accompanies the decision must correspond to the profile of the users. Depending on how AI will impact their work and life, but also on their maturity vis-à-vis this technology, not everyone will need the same granularity in the explanation.

To know the appetite of your users for AI, the best thing is to ask them the question through a short questionnaire. This will make it possible to detect the populations towards which it will be necessary to make a special effort to achieve genuine support.

Moreover, you won't give the same information to an expert or a novice. For example, for a medical diagnostic algorithm, you won't give the same information to doctors or patients. Doctors will need more technical information, patients more plain English ones. Workshops with your users and regular feedbacks are indispensable to fit your interface with their information requirements to trust your solution.

# B. Probabilities

By highlighting the relevant information, giving the user as much context as possible, it becomes possible to erase the feeling of no longer having any control over the decisions made by the machine.

The first information that will interest the user is to know how reliable the AI recommendation is. We too often set a default decision (i.e. threshold of 50% for a binary decision), and only give users the final decision: yes or no. Knowing the probability of a prediction can be a key acceptability factor. Indeed, depending on

<!-- PageBreak -->

whether this percentage is 60% or 90% for a binary classification, the confidence in your model's predictions will not be the same.

So instead of using the 'predict()' result, always get the 'predict_proba()'!

However here, it must be taken into account that the majority of your users are not scientists and therefore have a biased representation of probabilities, with a tendency to overestimate low probability events and underestimate high probability events.

Figure from : Khaw et al. 2021 https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008871

Thus, to simplify this notion of probability, they can be expressed not as a percentage, but in explicit terms. The reliability of the AI prediction or decision will can be "absolutely certain", "certain", "probable" or "very uncertain".

## B.1. Calibration

Some models (live SVM) can give you poor estimates of the probabilities and therefore make the interpretation of the probabilities unreliable.

We recommend calibrating your model or at least, check their reliability with calibration curves.

Lean more about calibration here:

https://www.cs.cornell.edu/~alexn/papers/calibration.icml05.crc.rev3.pdf

And on how to implement it with sklearn here:

## 1.16. Probability calibration

# C. Confidence intervals

Another interesting information to provide to the users: the confidence interval. This allows you to know on which subcategories of data the model is reliable, and for which, not so much. It is directly related to the variability in the prediction for a certain range of predictions and very much depends on how much data of each subcategories the model has been trained. For example, if a model has been trained with a lot of Caucasian faces and a few Asian ones, it will tend to be more reliable for the first class.

<!-- PageBreak -->

## C.1. Cross validation

You can get a first measure of the variability of your overall model performance by doing cross-validation (3.1. Cross-validation: evaluating estimator performance ), but it is not enough as it doesn't go into the details of performance for the subcategories.

## C.2. Mapie

You can use a toolbox called Mapie (MAPIE - Model Agnostic Prediction Interval Estimator - MAPIE 0.6.5 documentation ) which is a model agnostic solution that works for both regression and classification problems.

Source : Taquet et al. 2022 https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.12274.pdf

You can find a video explaining the solution here : https://crossminds.ai/video/mapie- model-agnostic-prediction-interval-estimator-614bc17e3c7a224a9090211b/

And articles here:

· With MAPIE, uncertainties are back in machine learning !

The explainability pillar consists in explaining the results (derived from interpretability) to the users of an Al solution (so that they can understand them and adopt the solution).

## KEEP HUMANS IN THE LOOP

It refers to the practice of preserving human involvement and oversight in the decision-making processes of artificial intelligence systems. This involvement ensures accountability and helps prevent potential biases or errors in Al-driven decisions. Moreover, by preserving the fundamental human need for control and agency in decision- making processes, it fosters adoption of the solution.

results.content: ## · And mitigating AI risks is a true challenge in business adoption Hallucination, bias, confidentiality: these are the risks and limits that are holding companies back from using AI, through a healthy respect for both the regulatory framework, and a context where the acceptable margin of error in decision-making is low. So what do we mean by this? · Hallucination: generative Als are based on a multitude of documents. When the next word to predict matches the truth, all is well. But otherwise? They must choose one option, and can hallucinate untruths with great aplomb. Users therefore need to be trained to use these AIs properly, and to verify every single claim they make. . Bias: they are rarely intentional, but algorithmic biases are based on data reflecting human practice. The system can therefore discriminate against a specific group of people. A major obstacle for businesses is to identify potential biases (lack of qualified data), raise awareness among employees and have the resources to do so (a dedicated inclusive team, for instance, or a taxonomy programmed with contextual information), and then deal with the biases. . Privacy: The confidentiality rules of GenAl, and ChatGPT in particular, are still poorly understood. Bear in mind that any data and/or code sent to one of these platforms is likely to be used for subsequent training, which raises issues of confidentiality of corporate data (or that of its customers) and intellectual property. Overcoming these risks is not an option, it's a sine qua non condition for some businesses. However, the adoption of AI itself is facilitated when it is designed responsibly from the outset: ethical standards reinforce confidence in its use; responsible practices in critical sectors such as human resources guarantee a positive and equitable societal impact; operational excellence prevents abuse and ensures that the AI is beneficial and reliable... Adopting a responsible AI is thus becoming a crucial approach to minimizing risk. ## . Key Issue ### How do we turn this AI revolution into a competitive advantage? We need new "software" to tackle this profound change in the way we work, and even in the way we do business. New responsible governance must overcome all the risks generated by the use of AI and generative AI. By evolving into an "AI-ready" business, organizations put in place the conditions that will enable them to meet the key business challenges of the future, and perpetuate their business practices and even their business model. It's a moment of truth for organizations: yes, there is a turning point ahead; yet it does not have to be a problem: by implementing a "responsible-by-design" approach, organizations are better equipped to deal with the risks -not just compliance risks, but also business risks- created by the exploding use of Al (see pillars). Ekimetrics intends to accompany this revolution with a simple, easy-to-understand framework to support these organizations in their AI transformation and the use of these technologies. In addition to the mechanisms above, there are a variety of relevant follow-up mechanisms and measures. One example is the use of independent expert groups or committees that can be in charge of monitoring the implementation and effective use of legal instruments (e.g. a convention) or the societal consequences from the uptake of AI systems. ## 08 CONCLUSION

In this primer, we have tried to introduce the main elements of the CAHAI's Feasibility Study, and we have provided some background information about the technical aspects of AI and the interwoven relationship of human rights, democracy, and the rule of law. We hope that, taken together, this material can function as a kind of launching pad for meaningful reflection on the prospects for a principles-based legal framework for governing AI research and innovation in accordance with the Council of Europe's stewardship of fundamental rights and freedoms, justice, and democratic values. Setting these transformative and increasingly powerful technologies on the right path for both citizens and wider society will demand well-informed, visionary policy-making and diligent anticipatory reflection. The Feasibility Study, and this supporting primer, offer first steps in this direction.

As the work of the CAHAI now enters the stakeholder consultation and outreach phase, it must be emphasised that the quality and success of this important effort will now depend on the wisdom and insights of as wide and inclusive a group of participants as possible. This reliance on you, the reader, at this critical stage makes good sense. The democratic steering of technology, and technology policy, is at the very heart of the human centred and values-driven perspective that places human rights, democracy, and the rule of law in the pole position for shaping the future of AI governance and digital innovation, more generally. It is, in fact, only through ample feedback and critique, that the voices of impacted individuals and communities can be properly heard and heeded. It is through scrupulous stakeholder consultation alone that lived experience can properly inform this cooperative endeavour to ensure the development of a sustainable technological ecosystem that safeguards the flourishing of the society of tomorrow.

## 09 APPENDICES

### APPENDIX 1: GLOSSARY

· Accountability: Accountability can be broken down into two subcomponents: answerability and auditability. Answerability refers to establishing a continuous chain of human responsibility across the whole AI project delivery workflow and demands that explanations and justifications of both the content of algorithmically supported decisions and the processes behind their production be offered by competent human authorities in plain, understandable, and coherent language. Auditability answers the question of how the designers and implementers of AI systems are to be held accountable. This aspect of accountability has to do with demonstrating both the responsibility of design and use practices and the justifiability of outcomes.

· Algorithm: An algorithm is a procedure or series of steps that provide instructions on how to take a series of inputs and produce an output. For instance, a recipe can be thought of as an algorithm that provides instructions for taking a series of inputs (i.e. the ingredients) and creating an output (e.g. a cake). In the case of machine learning, the algorithm is typically a series of instructions that instruct a software package to take a dataset (i.e. the input) and learn a model or discover some underlying pattern (i.e. the output).

· Algorithmic Audits: There are a variety of approaches to algorithmic auditing, which range from the targeted assessment of a system according to some metric (e.g. level of bias) to a broader approach that focuses on whether the system complies with a set of norms or regulatory area. While typically performed by professionals for the purpose of independent assessment, algorithmic audits have also been used by journalists, academics, and activists as a means of securing greater levels of transparency and accountability.

· Automated decision: An automated decision is the selection of an action or a recommendation made using computational processes. Automated decisions describe those that either augment or replace decisional work typically performed by humans alone. Most commonly, automated decisions are predictions about persons or conditions in the world derived from machine learning analysis of data about past events and its similarity to a given set of conditions.

· Outcome fairness is an assessment of whether the decisions or other results produced by Al are equitable, fair, and result in distributions of rights, obligations, and public goods in a just manner. Outcome fairness is also an evaluation of the values promoted or prevented by the use of AI.

· We can break down the fairness of an instance of Al as well by the perspectives of the stakeholders who affect or are affected by its use. Each instance of AI has a different and potentially shifting set of stakeholders. General categories include subjects, implementers, and societies.

· To establish subject fairness, we can ask if the person who is subject to a decision or action taken by or supported by an AI system perceives the process and outcome as justifiable and legitimate. To establish justifiability and legitimacy, the subject may need to know the details of how the decision or action was arrived at and what factors might have led to another outcome (e.g. a recruiting algorithm rejects a job applicant, which can be explained by showing that the applicant lacks a specifically named skill or credential). A subject also needs access to recourse if they disagree with the outcome (e.g. a job applicant has the opportunity to offer additional information or question the accuracy of the recruiting algorithm to a human with authority to alter the outcome).

· Implementer fairness can be expressed through accountability measures including processes of auditing and evaluation. Implementers are tasked with ensuring that AI systems are transparent and interpretable by those who use them and who are affected by that use. Prior to and during the use of AI, implementers should take social, economic, and political effects into account, being mindful not only of the perceived benefits of AI but also for the occurrence and risk of harm and who bears it. For example, the introduction of a criminal sentencing algorithm may produce more judicial consistency and/or streamline decision making. However, the same system may also reproduce discriminatory outcomes, such as where people of colour have received longer sentences for similar convictions as whites in white-majority countries, due to some feature of its design or the data it references. Where such conflicts occur, the functional accuracy or efficiency (if present) of an AI should be set aside and the algorithm design and data model should be thoroughly evaluated, including the decision as to whether to use it.

· Societal fairness carries a wider concern. A system whose use has potential impacts on the rights and privileges of individuals, groups, and/or the direction of society requires close attention by human beings and an open deliberative process regarding its use. Policy makers, scholars, and activists are tasked with proposing and critiquing strategies and actions aimed at promoting general well-being and social justice. When AI is used in either private or public sector settings (or both due to public-private partnerships), it potentially participates in preserving or contesting existing social, economic, and political arrangements.

<!-- PageFooter: page 38 -->
<!-- PageBreak -->

As such, AI should be subject to open and inclusive evaluation for its role in these arrangements, and the humans involved in its design and implementation should be held to account for their choices. Ultimately, the use of AI, like any tool, is acceptable only if it promotes improvements in the conditions of life faced by humans without causing harm.

· Generalisability: A model is said to be generalisable when it is effective across a wide range of inputs that reflect real world data, and in a wide range of operational contexts. If a model is not sufficiently trained on representative data it is likely to have limited generalisability when deployed in the real world.

· Intellectual property: Intellectual property (IP) describes the products of creative work and their legal possession. Common forms of intellectual property include copyrights, patents, trademarks, and trade secrets. Copyright is a form of IP that protects a creator's right to profit from the authorship of an original work such as a novel, musical composition, or painting. A patent is an exclusive but time-limited licence to profit from the invention and discovery of new and useful processes, machines, articles of manufacture, or compositions of matter. Examples include new medicinal drugs and driverless car technologies. A trademark allows a business entity to reserve the use of a word, name, symbol, or device, or any combination thereof, that identifies its goods and distinguishes them from goods produced by others. An example is the name "Twitter" and associated logos that uniquely identify and distinguish a prominent social media platform. A trade secret is any information that can be used in the operation of a business or other enterprise and that is sufficiently valuable and secret to afford an actual or potential economic advantage over others, such as the recipe for Coca-Cola.

### 'AI system' broadly defined

Recently, there has been a consensus on the meaning of the term'Al system'. The term Al system is included in the AI Act and is based on the OECD global recommen- dation. Briefly worded, an Al system can - for explicit or implicit purposes - infer from input received how to generate output. Like making predictions, generating content, making recommendations or making decisions. This output affects the physical or virtual environment. AI systems vary in their degree of autonomy and adapt- ability when deployed (after the development phase).

Based on current understanding, the term AI system refers to a wide range of applications, from simple (static) algorithms to complex AI or self-learning AI. In a recent explanation of the recalibration of the definition, the OECD explains, for example, that the model that forms the basis of an AI system (there could also be several models), can be either manually built by human programmers or automatically created, for example by unaccompanied, guided or self-reinforcing machine learning techniques. The OECD emphasizes in the explanatory memorandum that model adjustments are often part of the development phase and that the model is usually fixed during deployment. Different AI systems vary in their level of autonomy and adaptability in deployment. Traditional and simple software develop- ment, in which people have fully determined which rules are applied, falls outside the scope of the term.

The term Al system covers both applications that'only' make recommendations to people and applications that can make drastic decisions on their own. It is often the context and the embedding in a broader task or objective that determines the form of the output of an AI system. An example is a support system for car drivers. Such a system can'predict' that another car is nearby, then'recommend' the driver and warn him to brake. But the system can also be used in such a way that it inde- pendently'decides' to brake. In both cases, there is an Al system. The knowledge needed to deal responsibly with these systems, to be aware of their risks and effects and to make responsible decisions about their deployment is called'Al literacy'.

Guidelines from the European Commission will provide further clarification. Guidelines will be published on the practical application of the definition of an AI system. This will ensure further clarification, for instance through examples.

### Which AI systems stood out?

. Tech innovations. Impetuous and incident-rich launches of generative AI systems by big tech companies.

. Behavioural monitoring. Targeting customers and visitors via cameras in supermarkets, gyms and public transport.

· Algorithmic management. A management system for road authorities at Rijkswaterstaat.

. Housing. Use of Al and scraping for detection of housing fraud by housing corporations.

. Testing in education. The attainment test for primary school leavers, with an important role for adaptive testing.

. Public services. A system for filtering requests for social security through machine learning.

### What are the noticeable risks?

. 'Rat race'in tech. Big tech companies are striving for rapid market dominance in AI. Quality standards and risk management are under pressure.

· Abuse of generative Al. Technology is a panacea for malicious people. Risks such as cybersecurity are on the rise.

. Provision of information threatened. The use of Al systems in the production, moderation and consumption of online information has an impact on diversity and reliability - possibly with a major impact on public debate.

· Democratic control over Al. Governments are not suffi- ciently equipped to control the deployment of AI systems in the public sector. Incidents may therefore be noticed too late (or not at all).

. Discrimination in Al systems for selection. Profiling and selection systems, for example for fraud detection, are still under public scrutiny and detecting discrimination is often difficult.

· Timeliness of detailed regulation. It is questionable whether clear and solid product standards under the AI Act will arrive on time.

. Long transition periods. There is a transition period until 2030 for existing high-risk AI systems in the public sector.

. You cannot see the forest for the trees. There is a proliferation of frameworks and standards.

The technical documentation should be kept up to date, appropriately throughout the lifetime of the AI system. (72) To address concerns related to opacity and complexity of certain AI systems and help deployers to fulfil their obligations under this Regulation, transparency should be required for high-risk AI systems before they are placed on the market or put it into service. High-risk AI systems should be designed in a manner to enable deployers to understand how the AI system works, evaluate its functionality, and comprehend its strengths and limitations. High-risk AI systems should be accompanied by appropriate information in the form of instructions of use. Such information should include the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance of the AI system. Those would cover information on possible known and foreseeable circumstances related to the use of the high-risk AI system, including deployer action that may influence system behaviour and performance, under which the AI system can lead to risks to health, safety, and fundamental rights, on the changes that have been pre-determined and assessed for conformity by the provider and on the relevant human oversight measures, including the measures to facilitate the interpretation of the outputs of the AI system by the deployers. Transparency, including the accompanying instructions for use, should assist deployers in the use of the system and support informed decision making by them. Deployers should, inter alia, be in a better position to make the correct choice of the system that they intend to use in light of the obligations applicable to them, be educated about the intended and precluded uses, and use the AI system correctly and as appropriate. In order to enhance legibility and accessibility of the information included in the instructions of use, where appropriate, illustrative examples, for instance on the limitations and on the intended and precluded uses of the AI system, should be included. Providers should ensure that all documentation, including the instructions for use, contains meaningful, comprehensive, accessible and understandable information, taking into account the needs and foreseeable knowledge of the target deployers. Instructions for use should be made available in a language which can be easily understood by target deployers, as determined by the Member State concerned.

(73) High-risk AI systems should be designed and developed in such a way that natural persons can oversee their functioning, ensure that they are used as intended and that their impacts are addressed over the system's lifecycle. To that end, appropriate human oversight measures should be identified by the provider of the system before its placing on the market or putting into service. In particular, where appropriate, such measures should guarantee that the system is subject to in-built operational constraints that cannot be overridden by the system itself and is responsive to the human operator, and that the natural persons to whom human oversight has been assigned have the necessary competence, training and authority to carry out that role. It is also essential, as appropriate, to ensure that high-risk AI systems include mechanisms to guide and inform a natural person to whom human oversight has been assigned to make informed decisions if, when and how to intervene in order to avoid negative consequences or risks, or stop the system if it does not perform as intended. Considering the significant consequences for persons in the case of an incorrect match by certain biometric identification systems, it is appropriate to provide for an enhanced human oversight requirement for those systems so that no action or decision may be taken by the deployer on the basis of the identification resulting from the system unless this has been separately verified and confirmed by at least two natural persons. Those persons could be from one or more entities and include the person operating or using the system. This requirement should not pose unnecessary burden or delays and it could be sufficient that the separate verifications by the different persons are automatically recorded in the logs generated by the system. Given the specificities of the areas of law enforcement, migration, border control and asylum, this requirement should not apply where Union or national law considers the application of that requirement to be disproportionate.

The second and probably the most straightforward approach of getting a saliency map is using the backpropagation algorithm to compute the gradients of logits relative to the input of the network (note that in the backpropagation algorithm used for training the network, the gradients are computed with regards to the parameters of the network). This approach was first proposed by Simonyan et al. 2013 (Deep Inside Convolutional Networks: Visualising Image ... ). Using backpropagation, we can highlight pixels of the input image based on the amount of the gradient they receive, which shows their contribution to the final score:

Figure from Simonyan et al. 2013 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6034)

Springenberg et al. 2014 (Striving for Simplicity: The All Convolutional Net ) combined these first two approaches and proposed the guided backpropagation algorithm as the third way of getting saliency maps. In fact, instead of masking the importance signal based on the positions of negative values of the input signal in forward-pass

<!-- PageBreak -->

(backpropagation) or the negative values of the reconstruction signal flowing from top to bottom (deconvolution), they mask the signal if each one of these cases occurs. The following figure depicts the guided backpropagation algorithm very well:

Figure from Springenberg et al. 2014 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6806)

Here are some of the saliency maps produced by the guided backpropagation method. As can be seen - and reported in other works too -, this algorithm is quite good at capturing high-resolution and sharp saliency maps:

Figure from Springenberg et al. 2014 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6806)

We can easily see that the saliency map is a local gradient-based backpropagation interpretation method. Although saliency maps are mostly used for interpreting CNNs, as the concept of gradient exists in all neural networks, one can use it for any arbitrary artificial neural network. Thus, it could be considered as a model-agnostic interpretation method. A similar approach is used by SHAP gradient explainer that we saw earlier.

Finally, it is worth noting that there a couple of papers that have shown saliency maps are not always reliable. Kindermans et al. 2018 (The (Un)reliability of saliency methods ) demonstrate that data preprocessing, such as subtracting the mean and normalization, can make undesirable changes in saliency maps. Ghorbani et al. 2019 (Interpretation of Neural Networks is Fragile ) also show that saliency maps are vulnerable to adversarial attacks.

D.3.c.ii. Class Activation Mapping (CAM) and GRADient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM)

Class activation map (CAM) is another explanation method used for CNNs, introduced by Zhou et al. 2016 (Learning Deep Features for Discriminative Localization ). The authors of the paper have evaluated networks with the architecture similar to the Network in Network's architecture (Network In Network ). In these networks, the stack of fully connected layers at the very end of the model has been replaced by a layer named Global Average Pooling (GAP). GAP simply averages the activations of each feature map and concatenates these averages and outputs them as a vector. Then, a weighted sum of this vector is fed to the final softmax loss layer. Using this architecture, we can highlight the important regions of the image by projecting back the weights of the output on the convolutional feature maps. The following figure illustrates this process:

<!-- PageBreak -->

<!-- PageHeader: Figure from Zhou et al. 2016 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.04150) -->

An example of Class Activation Map. The figure is borrowed from Zhu et al. 2017 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.01829).

Grad-CAM is a more versatile version of CAM that can produce visual explanations for any arbitrary CNN, even if the network contains a stack of fully connected layers too (e.g. the VGG networks).

In order to get the Grad-CAM of a given image and a class of interest, we can take a quite similar approach to what we took in computing saliency maps; we let the gradients of any target concept score (logits for any class of interest such as 'human's face') flow into the final convolutional layer. We can then compute an importance score based on the gradients and produce a coarse localization map highlighting the important regions in the image for predicting that concept.

The following figure shows a visualization produced by GRAD-CAM:

GRAD-CAM visualization of an example image for the class of 'Dog'. The figure is borrowed from Selvaraju et al. 2016 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.02391)

As Grad-CAM can only produce coarse-grained visualizations, the authors have also combined guided-backpropagation with their method and propose Guided Grad- CAM. They simply do that by an element-wise multiplication of guided- backpropagation visualization and Grad-CAM's visualization:

from keras. applications.vgg16 import preprocess_input import keras.backend as K import numpy as np import json import shap # load pre-trained model and choose two images to explain model = VGG16 (weights='imagenet', include_top=True)

<!-- PageBreak -->

X, y = shap.datasets. imagenet50 () to_explain = X [ [39,41] ]

# load the ImageNet class names url = "https://s3.amazonaws. com/deep-learning-models/image- models/imagenet_class_index. json" fname = shap.datasets. cache (url) with open (fname) as f:

class_names = json. load (f)

# explain how the input to the 7th layer of the model explains the top two classes def map2layer (x, layer) : feed_dict = dict (zip ( [model. layers [0] .input], [preprocess_input (x. copy () ) ] ) ) return K.get_session () . run (model . layers [ layer] . input, feed_dict) e = shap. GradientExplainer ( (model. layers [7] . input, model. layers [-1] .output) , map2layer (X, 7), local_smoothing=0 # std dev of smoothing noise ) shap_values, indexes = e. shap_values (map2layer (to_explain, 7) , ranked_outputs=2) # get the names for the classes index_names = np. vectorize (lambda x: class_names [str (x) ] [1] ) (indexes) # plot the explanations shap. image_plot (shap_values, to_explain, index_names)

These examples were taken from SHAP's github that you can find here: GitHub - shap/shap: A game theoretic approach to explain the output of any machine learning model.

## D.3.c. Attention

For images, LIME and SHAP are not the most common techniques for interpretability. There are specific ways to look into the role played by different pixels in a CNN model for images classification. We will describe some of the here.

<!-- PageBreak -->

### D.3.c.i. Saliency maps

Saliency map is an explanation method used for interpreting the predictions of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). This is probably the oldest and the most frequently used method of interpretation in deep learning. Basically, the saliency map of an input image specifies parts of it that contribute the most to the activity of a specific layer in the network, or the decision of the network as a whole.

There are three main approaches to getting the saliency map of an input image for a CNN. The first proposed approach is using deconvolutional networks introduced by Zeiler and Fergus in 2013 (Visualizing and Understanding Convolutional Networks ). In this paper, to recognize which features (which are basically the pixels) in the input image an intermediate layer of the network is looking for, the authors have proposed a deconvolutional network that reconstructs the input from the activation of that layer. We won't go into the details, you can read the paper, but the whole process can be depicted as in the following figure:

Figure from Zeiler and Fergus in 2013 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.2901)

Here are some of the results of the reconstruction of the input image from the activations of the fifth layer of ZFNet:

Figure from Zeiler and Fergus in 2013 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.2901)

# 4- Explicability

As described in introduction, AI is a system, with users to take into account and an interface to build. Once you have access to what factor influenced your prediction/decision, it comes the time to explain it to your users. That is what explicability is. Knowing your users, understanding not only their needs but their reluctances, choosing the right level of information, giving them control and ability to give feedbacks, all of these techniques will ensure more trust and adoption of your solution.

# A. UX studies

You need to know the appetite of users relative to AI to deliver the right level of explicability.

With explicability, we enter into UX Design and question the preference of users in terms of presentation of results. The level of explicability that accompanies the decision must correspond to the profile of the users. Depending on how AI will impact their work and life, but also on their maturity vis-à-vis this technology, not everyone will need the same granularity in the explanation.

To know the appetite of your users for AI, the best thing is to ask them the question through a short questionnaire. This will make it possible to detect the populations towards which it will be necessary to make a special effort to achieve genuine support.

Moreover, you won't give the same information to an expert or a novice. For example, for a medical diagnostic algorithm, you won't give the same information to doctors or patients. Doctors will need more technical information, patients more plain English ones. Workshops with your users and regular feedbacks are indispensable to fit your interface with their information requirements to trust your solution.

# B. Probabilities

By highlighting the relevant information, giving the user as much context as possible, it becomes possible to erase the feeling of no longer having any control over the decisions made by the machine.

The first information that will interest the user is to know how reliable the AI recommendation is. We too often set a default decision (i.e. threshold of 50% for a binary decision), and only give users the final decision: yes or no. Knowing the probability of a prediction can be a key acceptability factor. Indeed, depending on

<!-- PageBreak -->

whether this percentage is 60% or 90% for a binary classification, the confidence in your model's predictions will not be the same.

So instead of using the 'predict()' result, always get the 'predict_proba()'!

However here, it must be taken into account that the majority of your users are not scientists and therefore have a biased representation of probabilities, with a tendency to overestimate low probability events and underestimate high probability events.

Figure from : Khaw et al. 2021 https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008871

Thus, to simplify this notion of probability, they can be expressed not as a percentage, but in explicit terms. The reliability of the AI prediction or decision will can be "absolutely certain", "certain", "probable" or "very uncertain".

## B.1. Calibration

Some models (live SVM) can give you poor estimates of the probabilities and therefore make the interpretation of the probabilities unreliable.

We recommend calibrating your model or at least, check their reliability with calibration curves.

Lean more about calibration here:

https://www.cs.cornell.edu/~alexn/papers/calibration.icml05.crc.rev3.pdf

And on how to implement it with sklearn here:

## 1.16. Probability calibration

# C. Confidence intervals

Another interesting information to provide to the users: the confidence interval. This allows you to know on which subcategories of data the model is reliable, and for which, not so much. It is directly related to the variability in the prediction for a certain range of predictions and very much depends on how much data of each subcategories the model has been trained. For example, if a model has been trained with a lot of Caucasian faces and a few Asian ones, it will tend to be more reliable for the first class.

<!-- PageBreak -->

## C.1. Cross validation

You can get a first measure of the variability of your overall model performance by doing cross-validation (3.1. Cross-validation: evaluating estimator performance ), but it is not enough as it doesn't go into the details of performance for the subcategories.

## C.2. Mapie

You can use a toolbox called Mapie (MAPIE - Model Agnostic Prediction Interval Estimator - MAPIE 0.6.5 documentation ) which is a model agnostic solution that works for both regression and classification problems.

Source : Taquet et al. 2022 https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.12274.pdf

You can find a video explaining the solution here : https://crossminds.ai/video/mapie- model-agnostic-prediction-interval-estimator-614bc17e3c7a224a9090211b/

And articles here:

· With MAPIE, uncertainties are back in machine learning !

· https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.12274.pdf

results.content: ## · And mitigating AI risks is a true challenge in business adoption Hallucination, bias, confidentiality: these are the risks and limits that are holding companies back from using AI, through a healthy respect for both the regulatory framework, and a context where the acceptable margin of error in decision-making is low. So what do we mean by this? · Hallucination: generative Als are based on a multitude of documents. When the next word to predict matches the truth, all is well. But otherwise? They must choose one option, and can hallucinate untruths with great aplomb. Users therefore need to be trained to use these AIs properly, and to verify every single claim they make. . Bias: they are rarely intentional, but algorithmic biases are based on data reflecting human practice. The system can therefore discriminate against a specific group of people. A major obstacle for businesses is to identify potential biases (lack of qualified data), raise awareness among employees and have the resources to do so (a dedicated inclusive team, for instance, or a taxonomy programmed with contextual information), and then deal with the biases. . Privacy: The confidentiality rules of GenAl, and ChatGPT in particular, are still poorly understood. Bear in mind that any data and/or code sent to one of these platforms is likely to be used for subsequent training, which raises issues of confidentiality of corporate data (or that of its customers) and intellectual property. Overcoming these risks is not an option, it's a sine qua non condition for some businesses. However, the adoption of AI itself is facilitated when it is designed responsibly from the outset: ethical standards reinforce confidence in its use; responsible practices in critical sectors such as human resources guarantee a positive and equitable societal impact; operational excellence prevents abuse and ensures that the AI is beneficial and reliable... Adopting a responsible AI is thus becoming a crucial approach to minimizing risk. ## . Key Issue ### How do we turn this AI revolution into a competitive advantage? We need new "software" to tackle this profound change in the way we work, and even in the way we do business. New responsible governance must overcome all the risks generated by the use of AI and generative AI. By evolving into an "AI-ready" business, organizations put in place the conditions that will enable them to meet the key business challenges of the future, and perpetuate their business practices and even their business model. It's a moment of truth for organizations: yes, there is a turning point ahead; yet it does not have to be a problem: by implementing a "responsible-by-design" approach, organizations are better equipped to deal with the risks -not just compliance risks, but also business risks- created by the exploding use of Al (see pillars). Ekimetrics intends to accompany this revolution with a simple, easy-to-understand framework to support these organizations in their AI transformation and the use of these technologies. We have therefore developed 7 pillars of responsible AI, designed to create this competitive edge (see next chapter). ## · Empower business with AI and GenAI solutions through responsible governance Anticipate future regulations, limit the risk of damage to image and reputation, improve the efficiency, accuracy and durability of models, all while generating value: to meet all these challenges, Ekimetrics has developed 7 pillars of responsible governance, which can be considered true operational and business tools. THE 7 PILLARS OF RESPONSIBLE AI AND THEIR BUSINESS ADVANTAGES 1. Security Ensure the security of personal and sensitive data. GDPR compliance. Data Clean Rooms: value of personal data. 2. Transparency Communicate intentions clearly regarding data and models. Improve trustworthiness and product adoption. Model cards are important for documentation, transmission, and reuse. Registries are probably needed for the AI Act. 3. Interpretability Provide access to the factors that influenced the decision/prediction. More control, easier to debug. Allows explainability. Required for some products in the AI Act. 4. Explainability Explain the predictions provided by the models, work on the user interfaces. Improve adoption/trust. Human agency. 5. Vigilance Avoid possible prejudice to the users' interests, exclude discriminatory biases. Scandal prevention. AI Act compliance. Potential new customers. 6. Robustness Measure and ensure performance and stability throughout the system lifecycle. Performance. Control. 7. Sustainability Limit the system's energy consumption and carbon footprint. Financial gains, simplicity, control, acceleration. ### TYPES OF SECURITY AI FAILURE: - DATA BREACH OR LEAKAGE - NON-COMPLIANCE - RANSOMWARE / MALWARE - PHISHING - FAKE NEWS - MODEL AND DATA POISONING ### WHO'S IN CHARGE? EXCOM DPO COMPLIANCE/LEGAL IT MANAGEMENT DATA TEAMS FINAL USERS

#### 3.1.2.C. Methods for reducing prevalence of inaccurate content

Developers have implemented methods to mitigate the risk of hallucinations (see section 4.1.1.C.). It is important to emphasize that reducing this risk necessitates high- quality training datasets. Developers can further enhance this effort by applying constraints or rules on how the Al model generates its output. Such rules can include ensuring that the content produced by the Al model aligns with established facts and ethical considerations. For example, developers may create a rule that restricts the Al model from generating content on certain topics or that limits the model to using only reputable sources.272 Developers can also engage human reviewers to assess the accuracy of generated content and make any necessary corrections or adjustments to ensure it reflects objective reality.

To improve the legitimacy of Al-generated content, some developers use a technique called Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG, see section 4.1.3.C.1.). This technique involves combining a generative Al model with information retrieval techniques to generate more precise responses. Microsoft's Bing provides sources linked in the text of its response and footnoted with a shortened version of their addresses.273 Bing uses real-time web searches to retrieve current information (with their links) and generate an accurate response using these contents. Other approaches are proposed. For example, Hugging Face's StarCoder, a code-generating Al model, provides a search engine that allows users to "search through the pre-training data to identify where generated code came from."274

Despite these techniques, the problem of confabulations is not easy to solve. A recent study by Nezhurina et al. revealed significant deficiencies in the reasoning capabilities of state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs), which were trained at the largest available scales and claimed to possess strong functional abilities.275 When presented with a simple, concise common- sense problem, easily solvable by humans, these models frequently failed to provide correct solutions. Furthermore, they exhibited strong overconfidence in their incorrect answers and often generated nonsensical, confabulation-like explanations to justify their flawed responses, making them appear plausible. Standard interventions, such as enhanced prompting or multistep re-evaluation, were ineffective in correcting these errors. The study calls for an urgent reassessment of the purported capabilities of current LLMs and the development of standardized benchmarks to identify basic reasoning deficits that existing evaluation procedures and benchmarks may overlook.276

#### 3.1.3. Opacity

Each of the risks detailed above is troubling, but they may be even more concerning because of the lack of transpa- rency into how generative Al models and their developers operate. This "lack of transparency"-or "opacity"-has two primary causes: the technical difficulties of understanding exactly how generative Al models produce their outputs, and a lack of transparency by leading model providers into their internal development and governance processes.
